items.title: Kenny Burrell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Gerald is always easy to work with so we talked about the music—it was not any, not any problem—and figured out what to do and so I had stuff with the big band.

ctx.x: Or was there any other, you know, mitigating factor? I mean, the fact that such a critical mass of the artists that went on to shape the course of jazz hail from Detroit is something that is significant on the surface, but that’s what we’d like to know if you have any insights into what contributed to that.

I don’t think I have any special insight. I think what I might say has probably already been said and said by people that are none musicians. That there was a migration from the south to places like Chicago and Detroit and Detroit in particular because of the automobile industry. And so a lot of black families, black people, came to Detroit looking for work and they found it. And they were able to buy some instruments for their children and as you know from speaking with Gerald Wilson it had a very good high…
Well, you’re right, Gerald Wilson spoke very highly of the neighborhoods and his situation, his experiences at Cass Tech….

items.title: Gerald Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Kenny used to come out every winter and he would do a class called “Ellingtonia”... Then when he became head of the jazz part, I was already there

ctx.x: And then they went and take, but you all have, like you know, like Kenny Burrell at UCLA and then bringing you in. How did that happen?
